newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: U.N. says Taleban offensive hinders peace effort.
newsitem.headline: U.N. says Taleban offensive hinders peace effort.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl said on Wednesday the latest Taleban offensive was a blow to his efforts to reconcile warring Afghan factions.

Holl said after meeting Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, head of the Taleban administration in Kabul, that the Islamic militia's new assault was at odds with peace negotiations held earlier this month by a U.N.-organised working group in Islamabad.
"I told Rabbani myself that the attack was a serious setback to the working group because one of the main issues we discussed was a ceasefire," Holl told reporters in the Afghan capital.

The Taleban launched an offensive against their opponents led by Ahmad Shah Masood and General Abdul Rashid Dostum soon after the working group, which brought together three Taleban and three opposition delegates, concluded three days of talks.
"So if three hours after the meeting of the working group, a fresh offensive starts, it is certainly a setback," Holl said.
The U.N. envoy said at the time that the Islamabad meeting had produced agreement that negotiations were the only route to peace, but a Taleban spokesman said the talks had failed.
Holl said Rabbani had told him the Taleban were ready to take part in a second working group meeting in February.
In this month's offensive, the purist Islamic militia has pushed back forces loyal to Masood, military commander in the ousted government, and Dostum, his ally, north of Kabul.

Dostum is now battling to keep control of the Salang Tunnel that leads over the rugged Hindu Kush range into the ethnic Uzbek leader's northern fiefdom. His troops have blown up a bridge and part of the Salang road to block the Taleban advance.
Masood's forces are trapped in their Panjsher Valley bastion northeast of Kabul, which they lost to the Taleban in September.
Holl vowed to press on with his peace efforts, even if they might appear to have slim hope of success. "The alternative is doing nothing and nobody wants that," he said.
